capabilities.target: Postgres database via service role, bypasses row level security; includes integration_tokens and support ticket tables
support_messages table, rendered back to the customer in the public support widget

inputs.source: Developer's direct prompt in the IDE chat (e.g. 'Show me the latest open support tickets')
Customer-authored support ticket message submitted through the public support widget, returned into the agent's context as query results from cap.sql_read

instructions.note: execute_sql permits arbitrary SQL under a service role that bypasses RLS, with no declared restriction to a ticket-only schema, query allowlist, or table scope.

controls.name: Per-call IDE approval prompt showing SQL
controls.decay_rationale: Approval is enforced outside the model and displays the literal SQL text before execution (raw_action review), so it does not decay with model capability the way a summary gate would. However, effectiveness decays with approval volume: runtime notes state developers approve many calls per session (approval fatigue, SAFE-T1403), and the prompt conveys SQL text only, not provenance (whether an untrusted ticket triggered the query), so a chained read-then-write toxic combination can be approved call by call without the combined effect being visible.

controls.name: Least-privilege DB role excluding integration_tokens
controls.decay_rationale: A DB role scoped away from integration_tokens and limited to ticket-related tables would make the sensitive table unreachable from this path regardless of model behavior.

controls.name: Secret-pattern filter on writes to customer-visible tables
controls.decay_rationale: A structural check on insert content narrows the path but can be evaded by encoding or splitting secret values across multiple writes.

controls.name: Pinned, hash-verified Supabase MCP server package
controls.decay_rationale: Pinning the exact package version and verifying its hash before install prevents a rug-pulled release from silently changing tool behavior; this does not depend on model capability.

controls.name: Delimit and label ticket content as untrusted data
controls.decay_rationale: Even if added, a prompt-level instruction to treat retrieved ticket content as data rather than directives weakens as model capability and injection sophistication grow.

findings.title: Lethal trifecta (TC1): customer ticket injection drives service-role read of integration tokens and exfiltration via customer-visible reply

attack_path.note: Untrusted customer-authored ticket content enters the agent's context when it reads open tickets via cap.sql_read
Injected instruction in the ticket content directs a further service-role query (bypasses RLS) against the integration_tokens table
Injected instruction directs insertion of the token values into support_messages, which is rendered back to the customer, completing egress

findings.residual_rationale: The only preventive control is a per-call approval prompt showing raw SQL (ctl.tool_call_prompt). Because it is raw_action, the rubric's floor restriction does not apply and the mechanical credit (-2 tiers) would move critical to moderate. Residual is held at high instead because the prompt shows SQL text only, not provenance, so a developer cannot tell that the query chain originated from untrusted ticket content; combined with stated approval fatigue ('developers approve many calls in a session'), the gate does not reliably interrupt this specific chained read-then-write toxic combination, matching the real-world pattern this case is modeled on.

evidence.observation: DB connection uses the service role, bypassing row level security, with a table of integration tokens in the same database
Customers write ticket messages through the public support widget; rows in support_messages are shown back to the customer, creating a customer-readable egress channel
The IDE asks the developer to approve each tool call and shows the SQL; developers approve many calls in a session, indicating approval fatigue
A single access token (service role) is used for all execute_sql calls, with no indication of least-privilege scoping

recommendations.action: Scope the database credential used by the agent to least privilege, excluding the integration_tokens table and restricting execute_sql to specific views/tables needed for ticket triage
Add a structural filter that blocks secret-like values (tokens, API keys) from being written to any customer-visible table before the insert executes

Change the approval UI to show provenance (whether untrusted content influenced this query) and require a distinct confirmation when a call chain spans a sensitive read followed by an externally visible write
Treat ticket message content as untrusted data with explicit delimiting and an instruction not to execute directives found inside it

forecast.watch_signal: IDE adds a 'remember my choice' / always-allow setting for tool calls, the per-call prompt is removed or narrowed to only novel-looking queries, or approval volume per developer per session keeps rising such that calls are rubber-stamped.

findings.title: Unpinned Supabase MCP server (@latest) exposes tool definitions to rug pull (ASI04, SAFE-T1201)

attack_path.note: npx resolves @supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest on every launch with no pinning or hash check, so the published package can change tool behavior or schema without review
A rug-pulled definition could alter or add hidden query behavior while presenting a benign surface
Same risk applies to the insert path, potentially appending exfiltration side effects

findings.residual_rationale: The per-call approval prompt displays the literal outgoing SQL regardless of which tool definition produced it, which would normally earn the full raw_action credit (critical to moderate). Residual is held at high instead because the artifacts show no package pinning or checksum verification as a structural backstop, and the same approval-fatigue condition from f1 applies: a subtly altered query is no more likely to be caught than an injected one under high per-session approval volume.

evidence.observation: args include '@supabase/mcp-server-supabase@latest', an unpinned floating version tag fetched via npx on each run, with no hash or signature verification declared

recommendations.action: Pin the Supabase MCP server to an exact version and verify its package hash before install; fail closed on mismatch
Add a startup check that diffs the server's advertised tool schemas against a known-good manifest and blocks or warns on mismatch

rating.rationale: The design lets an untrusted customer, via a ticket message, indirectly drive a service-role SQL read of a restricted integration_tokens table and a write into a customer-visible table, completing exfiltration (lethal trifecta, ASI01/ASI02). Inherent risk is critical: an untrusted source reaching an irreversible egress sink of restricted data. The only control present is a per-call developer approval that shows raw SQL; because it is raw_action it would mechanically earn a two-tier credit, but stated approval fatigue and the absence of provenance context in the approval prompt mean the control does not reliably interrupt the chained read-then-write pattern, so residual is held at high rather than the mechanical floor of moderate. A second, lower-confidence finding on the unpinned '@latest' MCP server package (ASI04) shares the same dynamics. Forecast risk rises to critical if the approval gate is loosened, removed, or if session length and approval volume increase further, which would fully defeat the one existing control.

limitations: This assessment reflects the declared design and configuration in the provided artifacts, not observed runtime behavior; no logs, transcripts, or live testing of the agent were reviewed.
No full system prompt was provided beyond the developer's example request, so instruction-level findings are limited to what the runtime notes describe.
The MCP server's actual tool schemas were not inspected directly; tool behavior is inferred from the configuration and the known execute_sql capability of the Supabase MCP server.
Approval volume and developer behavior are taken from the stated runtime note ('developers approve many calls in a session') rather than measured approval rates or logs.
